solutions.17: For every x ∈ Z, x − x = 0 is even, so R is reflexive. If xRy, then x − y is even; hence y − x = −(x − y) is even, so R is symmetric. If xRy and yRz, then x − y and y − z are even, so x − z = (x − y) + (y − z) is even. Thus R is transitive and therefore an equivalence relation.
solutions.18: Let f(a) = f(b). Then 3a + 2 = 3b + 2, so 3a = 3b and hence a = b. Therefore distinct inputs cannot have the same image, and f is one-one.
solutions.19: If f(a) = f(b), then 2a = 2b, so a = b; therefore f is one-one. Every image 2n is even, so no odd natural number, such as 1, has a preimage. Hence f is not onto N.
solutions.20: For every x ∈ Z, x − x = 0 is divisible by 5, so R is reflexive. If 5 divides x − y, then it divides y − x, so R is symmetric. If 5 divides x − y and y − z, it divides their sum x − z, so R is transitive. Thus R is an equivalence relation. The class [2] = {5k + 2 : k ∈ Z} = {…, −8, −3, 2, 7, 12, …}.
solutions.21: Write f(x) = (x − 2)² + 3. Since f(1) = f(3) = 4 while 1 ≠ 3, f is not one-one. Also (x − 2)² ≥ 0, so f(x) ≥ 3, and every y ≥ 3 occurs for x = 2 + √(y − 3). Therefore the range is [3, ∞).
solutions.22: Write f(x) = (x + 1)² − 1. On [−1, ∞), if x₁ < x₂, then 0 ≤ x₁ + 1 < x₂ + 1, so (x₁ + 1)² < (x₂ + 1)²; hence f is one-one. For any y ≥ −1, choose x = −1 + √(y + 1), which lies in the domain. Then f(x) = y, so f is onto. Therefore f is bijective.
solutions.23: For every a ∈ A, a − a = 0 is even, so R is reflexive. If a − b is even, then b − a is even, so R is symmetric. If a − b and b − c are even, then a − c is even, so R is transitive. Thus R is an equivalence relation. The distinct classes are [1] = [3] = {1, 3} and [2] = [4] = {2, 4}. Hence A/R = {{1, 3}, {2, 4}}.
solutions.24: (a) The domain is {P, Q, R, S} and the codomain is {101, 102, 103, 104}. (b) The four students have four different images, so f is one-one. (c) Every locker in the codomain is assigned to a student, so f is onto. Therefore f is bijective.

notes.subtitle: Equivalence Relations, One-One & Onto Functions

concepts.title: Relation on a set
concepts.text: A relation R on A is any subset of A × A. Its ordered pairs determine which elements are related, so the order of each pair matters.

concepts.title: Three relation properties
concepts.text: Reflexive means every a is related to itself, symmetric means aRb forces bRa, and transitive means aRb together with bRc forces aRc.

concepts.title: Equivalence relation
concepts.text: A relation that is reflexive, symmetric and transitive is an equivalence relation. Its equivalence classes partition the set into disjoint groups.

concepts.title: One-one and onto
concepts.text: A one-one function never gives the same image to two different inputs. An onto function reaches every element of its stated codomain.

concepts.title: Bijective function
concepts.text: A function that is both one-one and onto is bijective. Always use the stated domain and codomain when testing these properties.

formulas: Reflexive: (a, a) ∈ R for every a ∈ A
Onto: for every y in the codomain, there exists x in the domain such that f(x) = y
method: For a relation, test reflexivity, symmetry and transitivity separately and state a counterexample whenever a property fails.
To test one-one algebraically, start with f(a) = f(b) and try to deduce a = b.
To test onto, set y = f(x), solve for x and check that the resulting x belongs to the domain for every codomain value y.
For an equivalence relation, form classes by collecting every element related to a chosen representative and remove duplicate classes.

example.question: On Z, define xRy if x − y is divisible by 4. Show that R is an equivalence relation and find [1].
steps: Since x − x = 0 is divisible by 4, R is reflexive.
Divisibility of x − y by 4 implies divisibility of y − x, so R is symmetric.
If 4 divides x − y and y − z, it divides their sum x − z, so R is transitive.
example.answer: R is an equivalence relation and [1] = {4k + 1 : k ∈ Z} = {…, −7, −3, 1, 5, 9, …}.

practice.question: On A = {1, 2}, is R = {(1, 1), (2, 2)} an equivalence relation?
practice.answer: Yes; it is reflexive, symmetric and transitive.

practice.question: State which property fails for ≤ on R.
Test whether f: R → R, f(x) = 5x − 1, is one-one.
practice.answer: It is one-one because f(a) = f(b) gives 5a − 1 = 5b − 1 and hence a = b.

practice.question: Test whether f: R → [0, ∞), f(x) = x², is one-one and onto.
practice.answer: It is onto but not one-one, since f(a) = f(−a).

practice.question: For xRy ⇔ x − y is divisible by 3 on Z, write [0], [1] and [2].
Show that f: [0, ∞) → [1, ∞), f(x) = x² + 1, is bijective.
practice.answer: It is strictly increasing on [0, ∞), hence one-one; for each y ≥ 1, x = √(y − 1) gives f(x) = y, hence it is onto.

tips: One counterexample is enough to disprove a relation property.
Do not confuse range with codomain when checking onto.
A function can be one-one without being onto, or onto without being one-one.
Equal equivalence classes should be written only once in the quotient set.
Binary operations and composition of functions are not included in the 2026–27 summative scope for this chapter.

notes.subtitle: Principal Values, Domains, Ranges & Graphs

concepts.title: Why principal branches are needed
concepts.text: Trigonometric functions are periodic and not one-one on R. Restricting them to suitable intervals makes their inverses functions with one principal value for each input.

concepts.title: Sine and cosine inverses
concepts.text: sin⁻¹ maps [−1, 1] to [−π/2, π/2], while cos⁻¹ maps [−1, 1] to [0, π]. These ranges decide the correct quadrant.

concepts.title: Tangent and cotangent inverses
concepts.text: tan⁻¹ has domain R and range (−π/2, π/2). With the NCERT convention, cot⁻¹ has domain R and range (0, π).

concepts.title: Composition requires care
concepts.text: sin(sin⁻¹x) = x on [−1, 1], but sin⁻¹(sin θ) equals θ only when θ already lies in the principal range of sin⁻¹.

concepts.title: Graphs
concepts.text: The graph of an inverse function is the reflection of the restricted original graph in y = x. Endpoints and asymptotes follow from the principal range.

formulas: tan⁻¹x + tan⁻¹(1/x) = π/2 for x > 0 and −π/2 for x < 0
tan⁻¹u + tan⁻¹v = tan⁻¹((u + v)/(1 − uv)), with quadrant adjustment when required
method: Write the principal-value range of the inverse function before evaluating an angle.
Replace a non-principal angle by a coterminal or allied angle having the same trigonometric value inside that range.
For algebraic expressions, draw a right triangle after setting θ equal to the inverse-trigonometric expression.
When adding inverse tangents, calculate the tangent of the sum and then use signs and size to select the correct principal angle.

example.question: Find the principal value of sin⁻¹(sin(5π/6)).
steps: The angle π/6 lies in the principal range of sin⁻¹.

tips: sin⁻¹x means inverse sine, not 1/(sin x).
Never return an angle outside the stated principal-value range.
The endpoints ±π/2 are excluded from the range of tan⁻¹.
Check the sign of every square root from the principal quadrant.
For an inverse-tangent sum, a tangent value alone does not determine the quadrant.

notes.subtitle: Operations, Transpose, Symmetry & Invertibility

concepts.title: Order and equality
concepts.text: An m × n matrix has m rows and n columns. Two matrices are equal only when their orders match and all corresponding entries are equal.

concepts.title: Matrix operations
concepts.text: Addition requires equal orders. The product AB exists when the number of columns of A equals the number of rows of B, and its entries are row-by-column products.

concepts.title: Transpose and special matrices
concepts.text: Transposition swaps rows and columns. A symmetric matrix satisfies Aᵀ = A, while a skew-symmetric matrix satisfies Aᵀ = −A and therefore has zero diagonal entries.

concepts.title: Non-commutativity
concepts.text: Even when both AB and BA exist, they need not be equal. Non-zero matrices can also multiply to the zero matrix.

concepts.title: Inverse
concepts.text: An inverse A⁻¹, if it exists, satisfies AA⁻¹ = A⁻¹A = I. The inverse of a square matrix is unique.

formulas: AB is defined when columns of A = rows of B
method: Write the order of each matrix and check compatibility before adding or multiplying.
For a product entry, pair one complete row of the first matrix with one complete column of the second.
When transposing a product, reverse the factor order as well as transposing each factor.
To split a square matrix, compute ½(A + Aᵀ) and ½(A − Aᵀ), then verify their symmetry properties.

example.question: Express A = [2 3; −1 4] as the sum of a symmetric and a skew-symmetric matrix.
example.answer: A = [2 1; 1 4] + [0 2; −2 0], the required symmetric and skew-symmetric parts.

practice.question: State the order of [1 0 −2; 3 4 5].
Find the transpose of [1 2 3; 4 5 6].
For A = [1 2; 0 1] and B = [1 0; 3 1], find AB.
Find X if 3X = [6 −3; 9 12].
Split A = [1 4; 2 3] into its symmetric and skew-symmetric parts.

tips: Matrix multiplication is row by column, not entry by entry.
AB and BA may have different orders or one may not exist.
In (AB)ᵀ, reverse the order to BᵀAᵀ.
A skew-symmetric real matrix always has zero diagonal entries.
Do not cancel a matrix factor unless the required inverse is known to exist.

notes.subtitle: Properties, Adjoint, Area & Linear Systems

concepts.title: Determinant and expansion
concepts.text: A determinant assigns a scalar to a square matrix. For order 3, expand along the row or column that makes the arithmetic shortest.

concepts.title: Minors and cofactors
concepts.text: The minor Mᵢⱼ is obtained by deleting row i and column j. The cofactor Aᵢⱼ = (−1)ⁱ⁺ʲMᵢⱼ carries the alternating sign pattern.

concepts.title: Determinant properties
concepts.text: Interchanging two rows changes the sign; equal or proportional rows give zero; and adding a multiple of one row to another leaves the value unchanged.

concepts.title: Adjoint and inverse
concepts.text: The adjoint is the transpose of the cofactor matrix. A square matrix is invertible exactly when its determinant is non-zero.

concepts.title: Applications
concepts.text: Determinants give triangle areas and diagnose linear systems. A non-zero coefficient determinant guarantees a unique solution.

formulas: Area of triangle = ½|x₁(y₂ − y₃) + x₂(y₃ − y₁) + x₃(y₁ − y₂)|
method: Look for zeros, equal rows, proportional rows or a useful row operation before expanding a determinant.
For cofactors, write the checkerboard signs +, −, +; −, +, −; +, −, + before calculating minors.
To find an inverse, compute the determinant first; stop if it is zero, otherwise transpose the cofactor matrix and divide by the determinant.
For a linear system AX = B, establish |A| ≠ 0, calculate A⁻¹ and then use X = A⁻¹B.

steps: The cofactor matrix is [1 −1; −1 2], which is already symmetric.

tips: A determinant is a number; a matrix is an array.
The cofactor sign depends on i + j, not on the sign of the entry.
Use determinant properties before a long expansion.
